plan.concept: How the RANSAC algorithm robustly fits a model by separating true data points (inliers) from noise and anomalies (outliers).
learningObjectives: After engaging with this figure, the student will understand how outlier data points distort standard least-squares regression line fits.
The student will be able to explain how RANSAC uses a distance threshold to classify points as inliers (blue) or outliers (white).
The student will be able to describe why fitting a model exclusively to the consensus set (inliers) yields a highly accurate result despite heavy noise.
plan.keyInsight: Standard regression gets dragged away by outliers, but RANSAC successfully ignores them by finding a consensus group of points that all agree on the same model.

interactions.label: Fitting Method
interactions.effect: Toggles between standard Least Squares (which uses all points) and RANSAC (which only fits to inliers).
interactions.teaches: The fundamental difference in sensitivity to outliers between standard regression and robust estimation.

interactions.effect: Adds or removes highly noisy outlier points (white circles) on the right side of the plot.
interactions.teaches: How increasing the ratio of outliers degrades standard regression while RANSAC remains completely stable.

interactions.effect: Adjusts the width of the tolerance band around the model. Points within this band turn blue (inliers); points outside turn white (outliers).
interactions.teaches: How the consensus threshold parameter determines which points are allowed to influence the final model estimate.

demo_steps.title: The Problem with Least Squares
demo_steps.narration: Look at the red line when using standard Least Squares with outliers present. Notice how the three white outlier points on the right pull the red line downward, causing it to misalign with the main trend of the blue points. This shows how highly sensitive standard fitting is to anomalous data.
demo_steps.focus: The misalignment between the red line and the diagonal progression of the blue points due to the pulling effect of the outliers.

demo_steps.title: Enter RANSAC Robustness
demo_steps.narration: Now switch the fitting method to RANSAC. See how the algorithm identifies the consensus set of blue inliers and completely ignores the white outlier points. The resulting red line now perfectly tracks the true diagonal trend of the data.
demo_steps.focus: The red line snapping back to perfectly align with the blue points, ignoring the white points entirely.

demo_steps.title: Testing the Limits of Noise
demo_steps.narration: Increase the number of outliers to the maximum. Notice that even with a heavy swarm of random noise points, the RANSAC line remains stable and accurate, whereas a standard fit would be completely ruined.
demo_steps.focus: The stability of the red line even as the number of white outlier points on the right increases.

demo_steps.title: The Role of the Threshold
demo_steps.narration: Adjust the inlier threshold slider. If you make it too narrow, valid points are rejected as outliers; if you make it too wide, outliers start getting accepted (turning blue) and corrupting the line. Finding the right balance is key to robust estimation.
demo_steps.focus: How points change color between blue (inlier) and white (outlier) as the threshold tolerance band expands or contracts.

plan.reconstructionNotes: A simple 2D scatter plot with a horizontal X-axis and vertical Y-axis, both terminating in arrows. The main trend is a diagonal line of blue dots (filled with light blue, solid black borders) running from bottom-left to top-right. A cluster of outliers (unfilled white circles with black borders) is located on the right side, significantly below the main diagonal trend. A thick red line represents the fitted model. When in RANSAC mode, the red line aligns with the blue circles; when in Least Squares mode, the red line is pulled down towards the white circles. If the threshold slider is adjusted, a faint shaded band should appear around the red line showing the inlier tolerance zone.
